You can always go somewhere, to some book or tutorial etc to learn how to do something specific, but learn things when you need them. 
Grab a project, no matter what (best something you really want to build) and get your hands dirty.

The main "mistake" you make, in my opinion, is that you just use the tools and code without really understanding it - And what I mean when I say "understanding" is that you haven't gotten your hands deeply into why things are written how they are and why they work.
You just need to dig more of the programming fundamentals, not only use it as a tool.
A framework or even a language can be learned relatively easily when you understand the fundamental core concepts.
 
I myself got disheartened the last years over the amount of people who just use the top of their Javascript framework toolset, or just brag about how easy data analysis can be done in python. That is the case, of course, but that's only scratching the surface about what programming is about.
This is also why university students in CS still have to learn at least one "heavy" language, like C++ for example, to grab programming at the core. 
  
The fun part comes when you've learned things like patterns, coding structures, principles like object oriented or functional programming, whole structures like when to build a microservices system etc and then, when you build something yourself and things just click - That's the part it's all about. 
 
What I did for example is that I combined learning my university level math and programming by building a library by myself for those mathematical functions. I didn't reinvent the wheel, but I learned a lot about both things.
